# CHAPTER 1:Introduction {#sec-intro}

## Background and Problem Statement {#sec-background}

Market research helps businesses understand what customers want. But it is expensive. A professional study usually costs between \$8,000 and \$15,000 [@lin2026]. Most small businesses in the San Gabriel Valley (SGV) cannot pay that. So they make big decisions, like pricing, new products, or where to open, based on guesses.

:::::: stat-strip
::: stat
[\$8K–15K]{.num} [cost of one professional study]{.lbl}
:::

::: stat
[4]{.num} [SGV industries we study]{.lbl}
:::

::: stat
[\~600]{.num} [real people used as a benchmark]{.lbl}
:::
::::::

AI may offer a cheaper option. Recent studies show that large language models (LLMs) can act like survey respondents. When given a profile, such as age, income, and location, an LLM can answer survey questions in ways that often look like real people's answers [@argyle2023; @aher2023; @horton2023]. In marketing, researchers have used this to estimate what customers are willing to pay and how they see competing brands [@brand2023; @li2024; @wang2026].

There is a catch. AI answers are not always right. They can be too confident, too uniform, or biased toward certain groups [@bisbee2024]. A common finding is that AI tends to get the order right (which option people prefer most) but gets the exact numbers wrong (how much they prefer it). Dr. Lin describes this as "trust the order, test the level" [@lin2026]. This means AI research is only useful if it is checked against real data first.

Our client is the Tarkington Business Futures Institute (TBFI), a new applied "Do Tank" inside Cal Poly Pomona's College of Business Administration [@cpp2026; @tbfi2026]. TBFI wants to offer low-cost research to local businesses. It faces three problems:

:::::: card-grid
::: card
[👥]{.icon}<br>**Training doesn't scale**

Training new student consultants one by one takes too long.
:::

::: card
[🖥️]{.icon}<br>**No live demo**

Businesses want to see a working demo, not a slide deck.
:::

::: card
[💰]{.icon}<br>**Research costs too much**

Local businesses need research they can afford and trust.
:::
::::::

Our team is TBFI's first student consultant cohort. Our job is to build the tools that solve these problems, test that they work, and use them to bring in TBFI's first clients.

## Project Objectives (POs) {#sec-po}

The project has four main goals [@lin2026]:

::::::: card-grid
::: card
[🎮]{.icon}<br>**PO1. Build the Do Tank Simulator**

A browser-based training game that walks a user through a full consulting job: intake, research design, AI survey panel, perceptual map, and client readout. At least 10 rounds, plus a short version TBFI can use as a sales demo.
:::

::: card
[📊]{.icon}<br>**PO2. Build the SGV Insights Dashboard**

AI-generated customer insights for four industries: specialty food and beverage, ADU and prefab housing, cross-border e-commerce and logistics, and health and senior services. Includes perceptual maps, customer segments, and a trust report.
:::

::: card
[📣]{.icon}<br>**PO3. Run a digital marketing plan**

A landing page, LinkedIn and email content, and outreach to local chambers of commerce. We track the full funnel, from site visits to client meetings.
:::

::: card
[🎓]{.icon}<br>**PO4. Train the first consultant group**

New consultants go through the simulator, and we measure their skills before and after.
:::
:::::::

### AO1. Evidence Review and Data Setup (Alondra Rodriguez) {#sec-ao1}

::: ao-panel
[Question: What does current research say, and what data do we have?]{.q}
:::

This AO gathers what we already know. It reviews published studies on AI survey respondents and collects public data for each industry, such as Census ACS, County Business Patterns, and Esri Tapestry. The output is a short summary of the evidence and a clean data set that the other AOs can build on.

### AO2. Perceptual Maps and Customer Segments (Simran Kaur) {#sec-ao2}

::: ao-panel
[Question: How do customers see brands in each industry, and what groups do they fall into?]{.q}
:::

This AO turns the AI survey data into pictures that business owners can read at a glance. For each of the four industries, it will build two things.

**Perceptual maps** place competing brands on a simple chart based on how customers see them, for example cheap versus premium, or traditional versus modern. Brands that sit close together are seen as similar, and empty spaces on the map can point to gaps in the market. Maps will be built with multidimensional scaling (MDS), the standard technique for this kind of visualization, and each industry will use its own attribute set rather than forcing all four into one generic chart. We will follow the approach of Li et al. ([2024](http://localhost:3087/?quartoPreviewReqId=1790656796014&quartoPreviewThemeCategory=light#ref-li2024)), who showed that LLMs can produce perceptual maps that closely match those built from real customer surveys.

**Customer segments** group respondents who want similar things, such as price-focused shoppers or quality-first buyers. Segments will be pulled from the same underlying data using model-based (latent class) clustering rather than simple distance-based methods such as k-means, since latent class handles a mix of attitudinal and demographic variables better and gives each respondent a probability of belonging to a segment instead of a single hard label. Where practical, the maps and segments will be estimated jointly so both outputs describe one consistent picture of the industry rather than two disconnected analyses. Each segment gets a short profile describing who they are, what they care about, and how to reach them.

Because AI tends to get rankings right more often than exact numbers, the maps will focus on where brands sit relative to each other, not on precise scores ([Lin 2026](http://localhost:3087/?quartoPreviewReqId=1790656796014&quartoPreviewThemeCategory=light#ref-lin2026)). This AO assumes the underlying AI panel is directionally sound in aggregate; it does not, on its own, confirm that the panel holds up at the segment level, which is a known weak point for LLM-simulated respondents ([Bisbee et al. 2024](http://localhost:3087/?quartoPreviewReqId=1790656796014&quartoPreviewThemeCategory=light#ref-bisbee2024)). For that reason, only results that pass the AO3 validation checks will go on the dashboard, and segment-level findings will carry their own confidence flag rather than inheriting a single project-wide trust rating. The output is a set of perceptual maps and segment profiles for each industry, tiered by confidence and built into the SGV Insights Dashboard (PO2).

### AO3. Validating the AI Panels (Gabriela Raygoza Quintero) {#sec-ao3}

::: ao-panel
Asses the validity of large language model panels by comparing their response against the human benchmark.
:::

This AO tests whether the AI respondents can be trusted. We will give the same survey to three AI panels (Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini) and compare their answers to Dr. Lin's panel of about 600 real people [@lin2026].

We will use two main scores. **Krippendorff's alpha** checks whether different panels agree with each other, with values of 0.80 or above treated as strong and 0.67 as the minimum [@krippendorff2018]. **F1 score** checks how often the AI's answers match the human answers. Following "trust the order, test the level," we will first check whether the AI ranks options in the same order as people, and then check how far off its exact numbers are.

The result will sort each finding into one of three groups: **use as is**, **use for rankings only**, or **do not use**. This tells TBFI and its clients how much to trust each result on the dashboard.

### AO4. Consultant Training Performance Evaluation (Yushan Huang) {#sec-ao4}

::: ao-panel
[**Analytics Objective:** Evaluate changes in consultant performance before and after completing the TBFI Do Tank Simulator using standardized skill-checkpoint scores.]{.q}
:::

This analytics objective evaluates whether consultant performance changes after completing the TBFI Do Tank Simulator. The simulator is designed to provide new TBFI consultants with a structured environment for practicing a consulting engagement, including client intake, research design, synthetic-panel fielding, perceptual mapping, interpretation, and client readout.

Consultant performance will be measured using standardized skill checkpoints administered before and after simulator training. Pre-training and post-training scores will be compared to quantify changes in performance. The specific skill dimensions and scoring criteria will be refined based on the simulation-based learning and training-evaluation literature reviewed in Chapter 2.

The analysis will focus on the magnitude and direction of changes between pre-training and post-training performance. This approach provides a measurable way to evaluate the simulator's training outcomes while recognizing that changes in checkpoint scores alone do not necessarily demonstrate transfer to real consulting performance. The results will support PO1 by informing improvements to the simulator and PO4 by evaluating its use as a repeatable onboarding and training tool for future TBFI consultant cohorts.

### AO5. Marketing Funnel Analytics (Veronica Vega) {#sec-ao5}

::: ao-panel
[Question: Which digital marketing channels generate the highest rates of qualified sponsor inquiries and sponsor acquisitions throughout the marketing funnel?]{.q}
:::

The objective of this analysis is to evaluate and compare the effectiveness of digital marketing channels in generating qualified sponsor inquiries and sponsor acquisitions for TBFI. Marketing performance will be measured using key funnel metrics including website visits, inquiry form submissions, demo completions, sponsor meetings, sponsor acquisitions, and conversion rates.

The independent variable for this analysis is marketing channel source, including Search Engine Optimization (SEO), social media marketing, email marketing, referral networks, and paid online advertising. The dependent variables are qualified intake inquiries, sponsor meetings, sponsor acquisitions, and conversion rates. Funnel analytics and comparative statistical analysis will be used to identify which channels contribute most significantly to successful sponsor acquisition outcomes.

Baseline performance metrics collected prior to campaign implementation will be compared with post-campaign performance metrics to assess marketing effectiveness. Results from this analysis will support data-driven decision making and assist TBFI in optimizing future marketing investments by allocating resources toward the channels with the highest sponsor acquisition performance and return on investment (ROI).

## Significance of the Project {#sec-significance}

This project matters to three groups.

:::::: card-grid
::: card
[🏪]{.icon}<br>**Local businesses**

Get research they could not afford before. A bakery or a senior care provider in the SGV can learn what customers want without spending \$10,000.
:::

::: card
[🏛️]{.icon}<br>**TBFI**

Gets working tools, a sales demo, and its first clients. The simulator lets TBFI train new consultants faster, so the program can grow.
:::

::: card
[🔬]{.icon}<br>**The research field**

Gets a real-world test of AI survey panels. Most studies so far were run in labs [@argyle2023; @bisbee2024]. We test the method on actual local businesses.
:::
::::::

For our team, the project builds skills that employers want: working with AI tools, testing data quality, building dashboards, and running digital campaigns.

# CHAPTER 2: BACKGROUND AND ANALYTICS OBJECTIVES

This chapter reviews the existing research frameworks, models, and empirical evidence relevant to the analytics objectives of the TBFI project. The purpose of this review is to determine whether established research can support each analytics objective, assess whether the available information is adequate, identify the need for additional project-specific analysis, and refine the analytics objectives before proceeding to later stages of the project.

#### Existence of Well-established Models

### AO2. Perceptual Maps and Customer Segments (Simran Kaur)

**Analytics Objective:**\
For each of the SGV industries, this AO builds an MDS-based perceptual map (where brands sit relative to each other on attributes like cheap-vs-premium) and a latent-class customer segmentation, estimated jointly from the AI-simulated panel so both outputs tell one consistent story. Because AI tends to get rankings right more often than exact numbers, maps focus on relative position, not precise scores (Lin, 2026). Only results that pass AO3's validation checks go on the dashboard, and each segment carries its own confidence flag rather than a single project-wide trust rating. Output: perceptual maps and segment profiles per industry, tiered by confidence, built into the SGV Insights Dashboard (PO2).

#### Existence of Well-established Models

Perceptual mapping and customer segmentation are both well-established marketing research traditions, so AO2 leans on existing methods rather than inventing new ones. On the mapping side, Ries and Trout (1981) provide the conceptual basis: a brand occupies a position in the customer's mind relative to competitors. Hauser and Koppelman (1979) compared the main techniques for measuring that position and found multidimensional scaling (MDS) best suited to cases, like this one, where the relevant attributes aren't known in advance. Wanninayake et al. (2019) show a practical MDS workflow that AO2's industry-level maps will follow, and Bijmolt and Wedel (2020) go a step further, estimating brand positions and customer segments jointly in one model, which is the direct precedent for AO2's combined approach.

On the segmentation side, Wedel and Kamakura (2000) provide the standard framework for segmentation bases and methods, and Punj and Stewart (1983) remain the classic guide to cluster analysis. AO2 uses a more recent extension of that guidance, latent-class clustering, which a 2016 Journal of Marketing Analytics simulation study found more reliable than k-means for mixed attitudinal and demographic data, the kind this project will have.

The newer, more directly relevant question is whether these methods hold up on AI-simulated data. Li et al. (2024) found that LLM-generated perceptual maps closely matched human-survey maps in aggregate, supporting AO2's basic premise. But Bisbee et al. (2024) found that synthetic and real survey data can diverge sharply at the level of individual relationships (48% coefficient divergence, 32% sign-flips), which is why AO2 treats AO3's segment-level validation as a prerequisite rather than an optional check.

#### Adequateness of Gathered Information

The literature answers the “how” well: MDS and latent-class clustering are defensible, established methods, and there's reasonable published evidence that LLM-generated data can support perceptual mapping in aggregate. It doesn't answer the “does it hold here” question, no study covers these four SGV industries, and none tests LLM panel accuracy at the segment level specifically, which is exactly where Bisbee et al. (2024) found the biggest risk.

#### Need for Additional Analysis

TBFI needs its own analysis for two reasons: no published segmentation work exists for small, hyper-local SGV businesses in categories like ADU/prefab housing or cross-border e-commerce, and the general LLM-survey literature can't substitute for testing this team's specific panel on these specific industries. The maps and segments have to be built and validated against AO3's results before they can be trusted.

#### Assessment and Affirmation of Analytics Objectives

AO2 should be retained as written. The literature supports both the MDS-based mapping and latent-class segmentation, and supports estimating them jointly. Final measurable AO2: for each of the four SGV industries, produce an MDS-based perceptual map and a latent-class segmentation, jointly estimated from the AI panel, with every segment-level finding tiered by confidence per AO3's validation before it reaches the SGV Insights Dashboard (PO2).

### AO4. Consultant Training Performance Evaluation (Yushan Huang)

**Analytics Objective:**\
Evaluate changes in consultant performance before and after completing the TBFI Do Tank Simulator using standardized skill-checkpoint scores.

#### Existence of Well-established Models

Simulation-based learning and experiential learning provide an established foundation for evaluating the TBFI Do Tank Simulator as a consultant-training tool. These approaches emphasize learning through active participation in realistic tasks rather than relying only on passive instruction. This framework is relevant to TBFI because the simulator is intended to reproduce major stages of a consulting engagement and provide future consultants with opportunities to practice decisions and analytical tasks in a controlled training environment.

Research provides evidence that simulation-based learning can support the development of complex professional skills. Chernikova et al. [-@chernikova2020], in a meta-analysis of simulation-based learning in higher education, found that simulations can support complex skills such as problem solving, decision making, communication, and collaboration. However, the effectiveness of simulation depends partly on the design of the learning environment. The study emphasizes the importance of scaffolding and indicates that instructional support should reflect learners' prior knowledge. This finding is relevant to TBFI because incoming consultants may begin with different levels of experience in market research, analytics, and consulting. Therefore, the simulator should not simply present a sequence of tasks. Structured explanations, examples, feedback, and opportunities for reflection can help make simulator participation a more meaningful learning experience.

Similar evidence is found in research on computer-based simulation games. Sitzmann [-@sitzmann2011] conducted a meta-analysis of 65 studies involving 6,476 trainees and found that computer-based simulation games can produce meaningful learning outcomes. The effectiveness of simulation was related to the design of the learning experience and the degree to which trainees were actively engaged. These findings suggest that simulator participation alone should not be treated as evidence of successful training. For TBFI, the simulator should function as an active learning environment in which consultants make decisions, observe consequences, receive feedback, and have opportunities to revise their work.

Evidence from business education provides additional support for this approach. Faisal et al. [-@faisal2022] systematically reviewed 57 empirical studies of business simulation games and found that simulations were associated with multiple types of learning outcomes, including knowledge acquisition, cognitive skills, interactive skills, and behavioral outcomes. This research is especially relevant to the TBFI project because the Do Tank Simulator is designed around a business and market-research consulting engagement. Its purpose extends beyond teaching factual information. Trainees are expected to apply research and analytics concepts while completing consulting-related activities. The review also identified substantial variation in how simulation outcomes have been assessed, indicating that evaluation measures should be aligned with the specific skills the training is intended to develop.

Although the literature generally supports simulation and experiential learning, previous research also cautions against assuming that simulation automatically produces skill development. Gosen and Washbush [-@gosen2004] reviewed research on experiential learning effectiveness and concluded that the literature generally supports its educational value while also identifying weaknesses in the research designs and measurements used in many studies. For the TBFI project, this distinction is important. Existing evidence provides a rationale for using simulation as a training approach, but it cannot establish that the TBFI Do Tank Simulator itself improves consultant performance. The effectiveness of this specific training tool therefore needs to be evaluated using measurable outcomes.

Research on instructional games further suggests that learning outcomes depend on how the simulation is constructed. Wilson et al. [-@wilson2009] reviewed relationships between game attributes and learning outcomes and argued that the relationship between simulation features and learning is not automatic. Features such as feedback, interaction, challenge, and fidelity may influence different types of learning outcomes. This supports designing the TBFI simulator around explicit learning objectives rather than assuming that completion of the simulator is itself an adequate indicator of learning. It also supports measuring performance through multiple relevant tasks or outcomes when feasible.

A standardized pre-training and post-training skill checkpoint provides one practical way to evaluate performance change, but research identifies important limitations of this design. Marsden and Torgerson [-@marsden2012] examined methodological concerns with single-group pre-test/post-test designs and showed that observed score changes can be affected by factors such as regression to the mean, maturation, history, and testing effects. Consequently, a higher post-training score cannot by itself establish that the simulator caused the improvement. Experimental or quasi-experimental designs provide stronger evidence for causal claims, but a pre/post approach can still provide useful evidence of performance change in an initial pilot when its limitations are clearly recognized.

Pretesting itself can also influence subsequent performance. Pan and Carpenter [-@pan2023] reviewed research on prequestioning and pretesting and found that completing a pretest may influence later learning by directing attention and affecting subsequent learning processes. This creates an additional concern for AO4 because trainees could perform better on the post-training checkpoint partly because they have already encountered similar material. To reduce this problem, the TBFI evaluation should consider aligned but non-identical pre- and post-training tasks rather than simply repeating exactly the same questions or activities.

Training evaluation also requires a distinction between immediate training outcomes and transfer to authentic professional work. Bates [-@bates2004], in a critical analysis of the Kirkpatrick training-evaluation model, questioned assumptions about relationships among different levels of training outcomes. For AO4, an increase in a skill-checkpoint score may provide evidence of learning during training, but it should not automatically be interpreted as proof that a consultant will perform better in an actual client engagement.

More recent research on workplace training transfer reinforces the need to distinguish immediate training outcomes from later application. Ardondi et al. [-@ardondi2026] reviewed training-transfer assessment tools across workplace-learning studies and identified substantial variation in how transfer is conceptualized and measured. This suggests that a single overall checkpoint score may be too narrow if TBFI eventually wants to make broader claims about readiness for real consulting work. Performance scores could therefore be supplemented, when feasible, with additional evidence related to the application of skills beyond the immediate training activity.

Hjellvik and Mallam [-@hjellvik2024] provide additional evidence concerning simulator-based assessment and training transfer. Their research distinguishes performance measured under simulator conditions from performance demonstrated under a transfer condition and provides evidence that simulator-based competency assessment can be related to later performance. For TBFI, this distinction is useful because it suggests that simulator-based assessment can provide meaningful evidence while also showing why transfer should be considered separately. A consultant who performs well on tasks inside the Do Tank Simulator demonstrates competency within the training environment, while broader claims about client readiness would be strengthened by evidence from an additional or more authentic task when feasible.

Taken together, the literature supports the use of simulation as an active and experiential training environment while also showing why the outcomes of the TBFI simulator should be measured carefully. The strongest common themes are the importance of realistic tasks, scaffolding, active participation, feedback, reflection, and performance-based measurement. The literature also indicates that pre/post comparisons can document performance change but have limitations when used to make strong causal or transfer claims. These findings support the use of standardized skill checkpoints before and after simulator training, while suggesting that the specific scoring dimensions should be aligned with the consulting activities taught by the simulator and refined as the training design develops.

#### Adequateness of Gathered Information

The existing literature provides an adequate theoretical and methodological foundation for developing an initial evaluation of the TBFI Do Tank Simulator. Prior research supports simulation-based and experiential learning as approaches for developing complex skills and identifies active engagement, scaffolding, feedback, and realistic tasks as important design features [@chernikova2020; @sitzmann2011; @faisal2022]. The literature also provides guidance on the strengths and limitations of pre/post assessment and on the distinction between performance in a training environment and transfer to professional practice [@marsden2012; @pan2023; @hjellvik2024]. However, the gathered information is not sufficient to determine whether the TBFI Do Tank Simulator itself produces measurable changes in consultant performance. The studies were conducted in different educational and professional contexts, and none evaluates the specific combination of market-research and analytics consulting activities included in the TBFI simulator. In addition, the final skill dimensions, scoring rubric, and benchmark for satisfactory consultant performance have not yet been established. Therefore, the literature provides a foundation for the evaluation design but cannot replace project-specific performance data.

#### Need for Additional Analysis

Additional analysis is required to determine whether consultant performance changes after completing the TBFI Do Tank Simulator. The project will need to operationalize consultant performance through standardized skill-checkpoint measures that correspond to the tasks and learning objectives included in the simulator. Incoming consultants can complete a checkpoint before training and an aligned post-training checkpoint after completing the simulator. The resulting paired scores can then be used to examine the direction and magnitude of performance changes.

Depending on the eventual sample size, measurement scale, and distribution of the scores, an appropriate paired-samples analysis can be selected. Effect sizes and confidence intervals should also be considered rather than relying only on statistical significance. If feasible, rubric-based performance measures, rater-agreement checks, or an additional client-style task could provide complementary evidence. Because single-group pre/post designs have important validity limitations [@marsden2012], the initial results should be interpreted as evidence of measured performance change rather than definitive proof that simulator participation alone caused the change.

#### Assessment and Affirmation of Analytics Objectives

The literature review supports retaining the general purpose of AO4 but also indicates that the original objective should be narrowed and made more measurable. The earlier question, "Does the simulator improve consultant skills?" is too broad because it does not specify how consultant performance will be operationalized or how improvement will be measured. It can also imply a causal conclusion that a single-group pre/post design may not be able to establish [@marsden2012].

Based on the literature, the revised AO4 is: **Evaluate changes in consultant performance before and after completing the TBFI Do Tank Simulator using standardized skill-checkpoint scores.** This version separates the project objective of building the simulator from the analytics objective of measuring its training outcomes. It identifies consultant performance as the outcome, specifies a before-and-after comparison, and identifies standardized skill-checkpoint scores as the primary measurement approach.

The exact dimensions included in the skill checkpoints should be finalized as the simulator's learning objectives and scoring rubric are developed. The TBFI simulator is intended to expose consultants to multiple stages of a consulting engagement, so the performance measures should ultimately correspond to the competencies the simulator is actually designed to teach. Existing simulation research also supports evaluating applied performance rather than relying only on simulator completion or participant reactions [@faisal2022; @wilson2009].

AO4 therefore remains aligned with the broader TBFI project while becoming more analytically actionable. The revised objective can be addressed with observable performance data and analyzed quantitatively, while interpretation of the results can remain appropriately cautious about causality and real-world transfer. This formulation can guide the later development of the skill-checkpoint instrument, scoring rubric, and statistical analysis plan.

### AO5. Marketing Funnel Analytics (Veronica Vega)

**Analytics Objective:**\
Which digital marketing channels generate the highest rates of qualified sponsor inquiries and sponsor acquisitions throughout the marketing funnel?

AO5 aims to identify the most effective digital marketing channels for qualified sponsor inquiries and sponsor acquisitions. Therefore, established research frameworks and models for digital marketing funnels, customer acquisition, conversion rates, channel effectiveness and marketing attribution need to be reviewed. These models represent a theoretical basis for analyzing customer behavior and evaluating the marketing efforts of organizations. Website activity, inquiry volume, demo completions, customer interactions, conversion rates and acquisition figures are indicators of the performance of marketing channels and thus of relevance for the marketing funnel analysis of AO5.[@brand2023; @wang2026]

For digital marketing in particular, there are established frameworks such as the Marketing Funnel Model which plots the buyer’s journey through a series of stages. The classic model contains five stages of customer behavior (Awareness, Interest, Consideration, Conversion and Retention). As consumers progress through the various stages of the marketing funnel website visits and sales can be used to gauge awareness and interest, and conversions such as inquiries, demo’s, consultations and sales can be used to assess later stages of the funnel. The performance of the marketing funnel can be quantified in terms of the volume of traffic to the website, the number of inquiries and resulting conversions as well as customer acquisition costs and return on investment (ROI) measures.[@brand2023]

The AIDA Model (Attention, Interest, Desire, and Action) is one more of the marketing frameworks that can be useful to researchers by breaking down the processes of the customer decision making in the digital marketing space. As the Marketing Funnel Model above measures conversions at different levels of the customer journey, metrics will vary for each stage of AIDA such as counts of Attention, Interest, and Desire generated and the conversion rates and engagement metrics for Action stages (e.g. email marketing click through rates for people who have reached the Desire stage). For example, ROI and Conversion of leads to customers of search engine optimization (SEO), social media marketing, email marketing and paid online advertising.[@li2024]

Today’s customers are not taking a straight line journey to purchase. The Customer Journey Framework describes in detail how customers are interacting with a company’s various marketing touchpoints, both online and offline. An example customer journey would be: a customer sees a tweet from a business in their Twitter feed, they click through to the business’ website by searching for it on a search engine, they come back to the site via an email campaign a few days later and book a meeting by way of a referral from a friend.[@li2024; @brand2023]

A marketing attribution model also is used to assess marketing channel effectiveness. It assesses which marketing activity has caused a customer conversion. Common types of attribution models include first-touch attribution, last-touch attribution, linear attribution and multi-touch attribution models. All of these models are of relevance for the objective AO5 and thus can be of use for TBFI to determine which of the digital marketing channels are generating the most qualified sponsor inquiries and even sponsor acquisitions.These attribution approaches can help organizations determine which marketing channels are contributing most effectively to customer acquisition and conversion outcomes [@brand2023; @wang2026].

Measuring the deeper end of the funnel helps to provide better insights to see whether marketing efforts are translating into any business value. So, in addition to tracking website traffic and other metrics that measure awareness and interest, previous research supports the use of metrics such as lead generation, lead quality, conversion rates, customer acquisition cost and customer lifetime value to measure and track the performance of different marketing channels.Previous research supports the use of metrics such as lead generation, lead quality, conversion rates, customer acquisition cost, and customer lifetime value to evaluate marketing channel effectiveness.

Together, the Marketing Funnel Model, AIDA Model, Customer Journey Framework, and Marketing Attribution Models define the current state of understanding digital marketing funnels and offer means of measurement of performance of individual and collective online marketing channels [@wang2026; @lin2026]. Such as website traffic, quantity of inquiries, completion rates of demos, quality and quantity of customer interactions, conversion rates and more, enabling application of funnel analytics to TBFI’s online marketing efforts in order to measure and maximize their effectiveness.

#### Adequateness of Gathered Information

There is significant prior work that describes and measures the performance of various parts of the digital marketing funnel including customer acquisition and conversion, as well as individual marketing channels such as SEO, social media, email, referral and paid media. We draw upon a number of established frameworks and metrics that organizations use to measure and manage their marketing efforts. Importantly, there is substantial prior work on the conversion optimization and attribution aspects of digital marketing that can inform our research.Recent studies have also demonstrated the growing value of AI-assisted market research and advanced analytics methods for understanding customer behavior and evaluating marketing performance [@brand2023; @wang2026]. Although the prior work provides solid theoretical foundations for the study of digital marketing, however, there is no prior work that specifically focuses on the processes and activities used by TBFI’s sponsor acquisition efforts within the specific context of the organization’s unique customer journey and overall business objectives.

#### Need for Additional Analysis

While there is valuable information regarding the performance of digital marketing channels available from previous studies, in-depth analysis into specific organizations’ digital marketing channels is required to identify the optimal mix of channels to create the highest quality sponsor inquiries and conversions. This is because the behavior of customers, the conversion rates and how different marketing channels perform vary greatly between different industries and companies. Furthermore, researchers have cautioned that synthetic or AI-generated data may not consistently represent real-world customer behavior. Bisbee et al. argued that large language models may introduce validity concerns when used as substitutes for human-generated data [@bisbee2024]. Similarly, Aher et al. found that simulated responses may vary depending on prompt design and modeling assumptions [@aher2023].In the case of TBFI, in addition to general digital marketing metrics, specific project-related metrics such as website visits, demo completions, intake inquiries, meetings with potential sponsors and conversions need to be analyzed in order to gain insights on how prospective sponsors progress through TBFI’s marketing funnel and at which points of the funnel they enter and drop off. Such analysis can support data-driven marketing decisions and enhance return on investment from future online marketing efforts.

#### Assessment and Affirmation of Analytics Objectives

A literature review on marketing funnel analytics, customer journey analysis and attribution models has identified that for acquiring customers in today’s digital marketing environment it is most important to assess the influence of multiple marketing channels and to measure conversion instead of traffic. Furthermore, the literature also revealed challenges in attribution and data quality which have to be addressed in an organization-specific manner.

Research supports the use of marketing funnel analytics, customer journey analysis, and conversion measurement for evaluating digital marketing effectiveness [@brand2023; @li2024; @wang2026; @lin2026]. At the same time, previous studies identify challenges associated with attribution accuracy and synthetic data validity, reinforcing the need for organization-specific analysis [@aher2023; @bisbee2024].

Final Measurable Analytics Objective (AO5):

AO5 – Analyze the relative effectiveness of SEO, social media marketing, email marketing, referral networks and paid online advertising by measuring Web site visits, demo completions, intakes, meetings with potential sponsors, sponsor acquisitions and conversion rates throughout the marketing funnel for all sponsor acquisition outcomes.

The findings from AO5 will support the business-intake objectives of TBFI to identify which of the various online marketing channels are able to generate the greatest volume of qualified sponsor inquiries leading to sponsor acquisitions. Use of the data will allow TBFI to make optimal marketing investments to improve the overall performance of their marketing funnel and maximise efficiency of sponsor acquisition.
